title: The Horse That Named a Unit

pages.text: A girl carries a bucket of water from the standpipe up the steps to her classroom. She is tired, and she says she has worked hard. A scientist would agree. In science, work is done whenever a force moves something through a distance. Work done = force × distance moved in the direction of the force. Force is measured in newtons (N) and distance in metres (m), so work is measured in newton-metres, called joules (J). If she had stood still holding the bucket, her arms would ache, but she would have done no work on the bucket, because it did not move.

pages.alt: A flight of school steps with a full bucket shown at the bottom and again at the top, with an arrow marking the height it was lifted.

pages.text: Two students each carry a full bucket up the same steps. The bucket weighs 200 newtons and the steps rise 3 metres. Each student does 200 × 3 = 600 joules of work. But one takes 10 seconds and the other takes 30. The faster student is more powerful. Power is the rate of doing work: power = work done ÷ time taken. It is measured in joules per second, called watts (W). The first student’s power is 600 ÷ 10 = 60 watts. The second student’s is 600 ÷ 30 = 20 watts. A thousand watts make one kilowatt (kW).

pages.text: The watt is named after James Watt, a Scottish engineer who lived more than two hundred years ago. Steam engines already existed, but they wasted most of their coal. Watt redesigned the engine so that it did far more work with the same fuel. His engines soon drove pumps, mills, and factories. To sell them, he had to compare an engine with something every customer understood: a horse. One story says a brewer tested Watt’s engine against his strongest horse. Watt worked out that a strong horse could lift about 15,000 kilograms of water through 0.3 metres every minute.
sentences: The watt is named after James Watt, a Scottish engineer who lived more than two hundred years ago.

pages.alt: A strong horse walking in a circle to turn a pump, beside an early steam engine with a large beam and flywheel.

pages.text: Watt called that rate of working one horsepower. We can check it with the equations. A mass of 15,000 kilograms weighs about 150,000 newtons. Lifting it 0.3 metres takes 150,000 × 0.3 = 45,000 joules of work. Doing that in 60 seconds gives a power of 45,000 ÷ 60 = 750 watts. So one horsepower is about 750 watts, or three-quarters of a kilowatt. The unit is still used. The engine of a corn mill or a motorbike is often described in horsepower. A 10-horsepower engine has a power of about 7,500 watts, or 7.5 kilowatts.

pages.text: Long before engines, people used simple machines. A simple machine does not reduce the work to be done. It lets a smaller force do the job by moving through a longer distance. Loaders roll a heavy drum up a sloping plank into a lorry instead of lifting it straight up. The plank is an inclined plane, the same idea the ancient Egyptians used when they built the pyramids. A pulley at a well changes the direction of the pull. A crowbar is a lever. A cutlass blade is a wedge. Engines and electric motors came later, to supply the force.

pages.text: Every engine changes energy from one form into another. A steam or diesel engine turns the chemical energy stored in fuel into heat, and then into movement. An electric motor turns electrical energy into movement. No machine is perfect. Some energy is always wasted as heat and sound, and engines that burn fuel also release smoke and carbon dioxide. Look for watts on the labels around you. An LED bulb uses about 9 watts. An electric kettle uses about 2,000 watts. The generators at Akosombo Dam can supply about 1,020 megawatts of power. That is more than a thousand million watts, from falling water.

activities.question: In which case is work done on the object, in the scientific sense?
options: A boy leans against a wall that does not move
A woman lifts a basin of yams from the ground onto her head
A man stands still holding a heavy bag

activities.question: Two people do the same amount of work. Who has the greater power?
options: The one who takes the shorter time
The one who takes the longer time
They always have the same power

activities.question: What does a simple machine such as a sloping plank do?
options: It reduces the total work needed to zero
It allows a smaller force to be used over a longer distance

activities.question: Apply it: A pump lifts 500 N of water through 10 m in 20 s. What is its power?

activities.prompt: Arrange from lowest power to highest.
items: A student carrying a bucket upstairs (60 W)
